provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.name: AI Ethics
provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.text: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.name: Psycholinguistics
provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

provisionalSelectedCourseDescriptions.text: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.

Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.
